1.title: Bobbing and Swinging
1.text:
Bobbing and Swinging

The period is the time needed for one full cycle of motion; the amplitude is the maximum distance an object moves from its equilibrium position.

Our big question for this lesson: what are some types of repetitive motion? Let's start bouncing!

A mass bobbing on a spring and a swaying pendulum are examples of periodic motion. In each, there's one spot where the net force on the object is zero. That's equilibrium. Move the object away, and a net force appears that pulls it back toward equilibrium.

The period, T, is the time for one full cycle of the motion. The amplitude is the farthest the object gets from its equilibrium position.

3.title: Simple Harmonic Motion
3.text:
Simple Harmonic Motion

Simple harmonic motion is motion in which the force restoring an object to its equilibrium position is directly proportional to the object's displacement.

In Figure 1, the spring's force is directly proportional to how far it stretches. Hang a weight of m g, and the spring stretches a distance x. Hang 2 m g, and it stretches 2 x. So a weight of 0.5 m g would stretch it 0.5 x, half as far.

Pull the mass down and let go, and it bobs up and down through equilibrium. Any system where the force pulling an object back to equilibrium is directly proportional to its displacement shows simple harmonic motion.

4.title: Hooke's Law
4.text:
Hooke's Law

Hooke's law states that the force exerted by a spring equals the negative of the spring constant times the distance stretched or compressed: F equals negative k x.

Table 1 shows how a spring's force grows as it stretches: 1.9 newtons at 0.030 meters, 3.7 newtons at 0.060 meters, and 7.8 newtons at 0.12 meters. Graph it, like Figure 2, and you get a straight line. The force is directly proportional to the stretch. A spring like that obeys Hooke's law: F equals negative k x.

Here k is the spring constant, which depends on the spring's stiffness, and x is the stretch from equilibrium. On the graph, k is the slope. In Figure 2, rise over run is 8.0 newtons minus 4.0 newtons over 0.12 meters minus 0.06 meters, which is 67 newtons per meter. A steeper slope, a bigger k, means a spring that's harder to stretch. The negative sign means the force always points opposite the stretch, back toward equilibrium.

Not every spring obeys Hooke's law. Rubber bands don't. Springs that do are called elastic springs, and even they only follow it over a limited range. Stretch one too far, and it deforms, and the force stops being proportional to the stretch.

5.title: Energy in a Spring
5.text:
Energy in a Spring

The potential energy in a spring equals one-half times the spring constant times the square of the displacement.

Stretch a spring, and you give it elastic potential energy. The work you do equals the area under the force versus distance graph in Figure 2, and that's the energy stored. The area is a triangle: one-half the base, x, times the height, which by Hooke's law is k x. So the potential energy of a spring is one-half k times the square of x.

With that, plus kinetic energy from mass and speed, you can use conservation of energy to predict what a spring system does. In Figure 3, a mass slides back and forth on a horizontal spring. Stretched all the way, the energy is all potential. Zooming through equilibrium, it's all kinetic. Then it's back to potential at the other side. The total mechanical energy stays constant the whole time.

So Hooke's law tells you the force and the stored energy at any stretch, and energy conservation tells you how fast the mass moves at each point.

6.title: Example Problem 1, A Bag of Potatoes
6.text:
Example Problem 1, A Bag of Potatoes

Find k from Hooke's law, then the stored energy from one-half k times the square of x.

A spring stretches 18 centimeters when a 56-newton bag of potatoes hangs from it. Find the spring constant and the spring's elastic potential energy.

Step one: analyze and sketch. Sketch the spring, labeling its equilibrium position and the stretch. Known: x equals 18 centimeters, and F equals negative 56 newtons. The force is negative because it points opposite the stretch. Unknown: k and the potential energy.

Step two: solve. From Hooke's law, k equals negative F over x: negative of negative 56 newtons over 0.18 meters, which is 310 newtons per meter. The potential energy is one-half k times the square of x: one-half times 310 newtons per meter times the square of 0.18 meters, which is 5.0 joules.

Step three: evaluate. Newtons per meter is right for a spring constant, and newtons per meter times meters squared is newton meters, or joules. Is it realistic? The spring's force rises from 0 to 56 newtons, averaging 28 newtons. Work is 28 newtons times 0.18 meters, which is 5.0 joules. It checks out!

7.title: Pendulums
7.text:
Pendulums

The period of a pendulum equals 2 pi times the square root of the length divided by the gravitational field: T equals 2 pi times the square root of l over g.

A pendulum's swing is simple harmonic motion too. A simple pendulum is a heavy object, the bob, hanging from a string or light rod of length l. In Figure 4, the string pulls with tension F sub T and gravity pulls with F sub g. The part of gravity along the bob's curved path is the restoring force. At the far left and right, the restoring force is biggest and the bob stops for an instant. At equilibrium, the restoring force is zero and the bob is fastest.

For small angles, less than about 15 degrees, the restoring force is proportional to the displacement, so it's simple harmonic motion. Its period is T equals 2 pi times the square root of l over g.

Notice what's missing: the bob's mass and the amplitude! A huge pendulum, like the one at the start of the module, has the same period as a tiny one of the same length. That's why pendulums are great for measuring g, which varies a little around Earth.

testIt.how: Change the length. Mass and small amplitudes don't matter.

8.title: Example Problem 2, Finding g with a Pendulum
8.text:
Example Problem 2, Finding g with a Pendulum

Rearranged, the pendulum equation gives g equals 4 pi squared l over the square of T.

A pendulum 36.9 centimeters long has a period of 1.22 seconds. What's the gravitational field where it's swinging?

Step one: analyze and sketch. Sketch the pendulum and label its length. Known: l equals 36.9 centimeters, and T equals 1.22 seconds. Unknown: g.

Step two: solve. Rearranging T equals 2 pi times the square root of l over g gives g equals 4 times the square of pi times l, divided by the square of T. Substitute 0.369 meters and 1.22 seconds: 4 times the square of pi times 0.369 meters, divided by the square of 1.22 seconds, which is 9.78 meters per second squared, or 9.78 newtons per kilogram.

Step three: evaluate. Newtons per kilogram is the right unit for a gravitational field. And 9.78 is very close to the accepted 9.8 newtons per kilogram. This pendulum might be at a higher elevation above sea level. It checks out!

testIt.name: Find g
testIt.how: Tap to time the 36.9 cm pendulum in another place.

9.title: Resonance
9.text:
Resonance

Resonance occurs when forces are applied to a vibrating or oscillating object at time intervals equal to its period, increasing the amplitude.

To get a playground swing going, you pump it by leaning back and pulling the chains at the same point in each swing. Or a friend gives you pushes at just the right moments. Resonance happens when forces are applied to an oscillating object at intervals equal to its period. The amplitude grows! You also use resonance to rock a car out of a snowbank, or to bounce higher on a trampoline or diving board.

Small bits of energy, added in time, build bigger and bigger swings. Ever held a conch shell to your ear to hear the ocean? That's resonance! Background noise in the room hits the shell, and sounds that match the shell's natural frequencies get amplified until you can hear them. Resonance also amplifies sound in musical instruments and keeps clocks accurate.

So, what are some types of repetitive motion? A mass bobbing on a spring, a swinging pendulum, a pumped swing, and a ringing seashell are all periodic motions. Springs and pendulums show simple harmonic motion, where the restoring force grows with displacement.
